F26.quote: LLMs are used to classify AI-related events into three categories: AI incidents, AI hazards or unrelated events, as defined above. This classification is based on the event summary provided from Event Registry. The classification follows a two-step process: first, a smaller model (OpenAI’s GPT-4o mini) filters out events that seem unrelated to AI incidents and hazards; next, a larger model (OpenAI’s GPT-4o) reclassifies the remaining events to confirm whether they are incidents or hazards.
F26.claim: classification by LLMs into incidents, hazards or unrelated, from Event Registry's summary: GPT-4o mini filters, GPT-4o reclassifies
F26.date: 2026-10-29 (page undated; as fetched; describes the method 'since November 2024')

F27.claim: articles are classified by LLMs from their content; the event takes the most common label among its articles
F27.date: 2026-10-29 (page undated; as fetched; describes the method 'since November 2024')

F35.quote: This paper analyses live data from the OECD.AI Incidents and Hazards Monitor (AIM), classifying media reports into 14 themes, including synthetic media, child safety, cyberattacks, privacy, and health. It identifies three distinct patterns of media coverage – increasing, intermittent, and declining – and traces how media attention shifts across themes over time.
F35.claim: the 2026 paper analyses the monitor's data, classifying its media reports into 14 themes, with three patterns of coverage
F35.date: 2026-02 (OECD Artificial Intelligence Papers No. 53; PDF created 2026-02-09)

F36.quote: The findings reflect media and public interest rather than comprehensive or systematic tracking of AI incidents and hazards. Importantly, media reports capture only what journalists are aware of and deemed newsworthy.

F51.locus: §4 Draft definition of an AI incident
F51.quote: An AI incident is an event, circumstance or series of events where the development, use or malfunction of one or more AI systems directly or indirectly leads to any of the following harms: (a) injury or harm to the health of a person or groups of people; (b) disruption of the management and operation of critical infrastructure; (c) violations of human rights or a breach of obligations under the applicable law intended to protect fundamental, labour and intellectual property rights; (d) harm to property, communities or the environment.
F51.claim: the definition of an AI incident: development, use or malfunction leading directly or indirectly to harms (a)–(d)
F51.date: 2024-05 (OECD Artificial Intelligence Papers No. 16; approved by the DPC 2024-03-14)

F52.locus: §5 Draft definition of an AI hazard
F52.quote: An AI hazard is an event, circumstance or series of events where the development, use or malfunction of one or more AI systems could plausibly lead to an AI incident, i.e., any of the following harms:
F52.claim: the definition of an AI hazard: an event that could plausibly lead to an AI incident
F52.date: 2024-05 (OECD Artificial Intelligence Papers No. 16; approved by the DPC 2024-03-14)

F53.quote: Near misses are events that could have led to an AI incident and are therefore included under this definition of AI hazards.
F53.date: 2024-05 (OECD Artificial Intelligence Papers No. 16; approved by the DPC 2024-03-14)

F54.quote: Serious AI incidents are a subset of AI incidents and are intended to include substantial, material incidents. … An AI disaster is a serious AI incident that disrupts the functioning of a community or a society and that may test or exceed its capacity to cope, using its own resources.
F54.claim: the graded terms: serious AI incident (a subset) and AI disaster (a serious incident beyond a society's capacity to cope)
